newsitem.title: USA: U.S. West spot electricity prices rise slightly.
newsitem.headline: U.S. West spot electricity prices rise slightly.

text.p: Spot electricity prices in the western U.S. rose slightly Thursday amid confusion over transmission rates and capacity in the Northwest and on regional weather issues, market sources said.
"Prices have been falling all week, so I would expect the softness to return--maybe by the end of the week," said a trader.
Next-day firm, peak Mid-Columbia electricity was last quoted $16.00-17.00 per megawatt hour (MWh), up a tad from $15.50-16.50 on Wednesday.
California-Oregon border (COB) firm, peak power for Friday was quoted $19.50-20.00, up from Wednesday's $18.50-19.50.

Traders said gyrating offers from the Bonneville Power Administration (BPA), which began this week to distinguish between prices for electricity and transmission, have created some uncertainty in the market.
"It's the time of year when (hydroelectric) flows are down as well as loads," said another market source. "Bonneville is just testing to see what the market will bear."
In the Southwest, next-day Palo Verde (PV) was unchanged from Thursday near $21.00-22.00 per MWh.
Traders said the outage late Wednesday of a 361 MW unit at the San Juan coal-fired plant in New Mexico had no impact on the spot market. The unit was due to restart Friday.
Sources also said cooler weather in the Southwest or Northwest could impact prices, but noted that PV quotes would have to dip below $14.00 in order for northbound deliveries to become viable.
November PV was last quoted $16.50-17.00 per MWh, up from $16.25-16.60 on Wednesday, while November COB was quoted $17.50-18.00, up from $17.35-17.50.
